h1:
Songkhla 1-Day Itinerary
Old Town · Samila · Khao Tang Kuan
intro: Songkhla is genuinely doable in a single day — everything sits within a few kilometres of each other. Spend the morning walking the old town by the lagoon, eating local breakfast on Nang Ngam Road, then head to Samila Beach in the afternoon to lounge by the mermaid statue. Wrap up with the climb to Khao Tang Kuan once the heat eases and the city spreads out below you. This itinerary is walkable, unhurried, and comes with a backup plan for anyone who only has time in Hat Yai.

blocks.html: Songkhla's compact layout is its biggest advantage. The old town, Samila Beach, and Khao Tang Kuan hill are all within the main district — driving or riding between them takes 5–10 minutes. If you're flying into Hat Yai and transferring to Songkhla city (about 30–40 min), you can still comfortably fit everything into one day. We've ordered the plan around the sun angle and restaurant hours so you don't show up anywhere that's already closed.

blocks.text: Main Plan: Songkhla Old Town + Samila + Khao Tang Kuan

blocks.html: This route gives you a genuine feel for Songkhla — the waterfront old town, real local food, the sea, and a city panorama at the end. The morning is mostly on foot; the afternoon involves short rides between spots.

blocks.label: Morning
blocks.title: The Three Old-Town Streets — Nakon Nork, Nakon Nai & Nang Ngam

items.activity: Breakfast, Songkhla-style — Khao Stew at Kiat Fang or fish congee at Jao Ni, around Nang Ngam Road
items.note: Khao stew (rice in spiced Chinese-style broth with pork or chicken) is the city's signature breakfast. A bowl runs around THB 50–70. Popular spots sell out fast — arrive before 9 am to be safe.

items.activity: Walk Nang Ngam, Nakon Nai and Nakon Nork roads — Sino-Portuguese shophouses, old mansions, street art
items.note: The three streets run parallel and connect at each end, making a natural loop. The total walking distance is an easy 1.5 km. Dozens of buildings are over 100 years old and make for great photos.

items.activity: Stop by the Songkhla National Museum on Wichianchom Road — a century-old colonial building worth a look inside
items.note: Closed Mondays, Tuesdays and public holidays. Entry for Thai nationals is a few dozen baht. If it falls on a closed day, photograph the exterior and move on.

items.activity: Coffee break in a heritage cafe — The Stand Brew, Lyn's The Shanghai Cafe, or grab a signature clay-pot ice cream on Nang Ngam Road
items.note: The clay-pot ice cream (served in a small earthenware jar) is a Songkhla old-town staple. It costs next to nothing and is the perfect cool-down before the midday heat sets in.

blocks.label: Afternoon
blocks.title: Samila Beach + Laem Son On Headland

items.activity: Lunch — seafood or southern Thai food near Samila Beach
items.note: There are several seafood restaurants and rice-and-curry shops along the Samila seafront. Fried fish, sour curry, and mud crab are the obvious picks here.

items.activity: Walk Samila Beach, photograph the golden mermaid statue and the cat-and-rat sculpture
items.note: The golden mermaid is Songkhla's iconic symbol. The beach has a row of casuarina pines that give decent shade for sitting. The afternoon sun is still strong — bring an umbrella or hat.

items.activity: Continue to Laem Son On headland for the two-sea viewpoint and the observation bridge
items.note: Laem Son On is right next to Samila — a 5-min drive. From here you can see both the Gulf of Thailand and Songkhla Lake in the same frame.

blocks.label: Evening
blocks.title: Khao Tang Kuan — Finish with a City Panorama

items.activity: Head up Khao Tang Kuan — take the incline lift at the front of the hill or climb the Naga staircase at the back
items.note: The incline lift costs around THB 30 for adults and THB 20 for children; it runs approximately 08:30–18:00. The ride takes just a few minutes. Check closing times before you go, especially if you're aiming for sunset.

items.activity: See the twin chedis and take in the 360-degree view of Songkhla city from the summit
items.note: From the top you can see the whole city, the lake, and the Gulf of Thailand. The light is softer in the late afternoon and is even better if you catch the sun going down.

items.activity: Descend and find dinner — either back in the old town for more seafood, or head to Hat Yai for the night market
items.note: If you're staying in Hat Yai, the drive back takes about 30–40 min. The Hat Yai night market makes a good second dinner stop.

blocks.title: Timing tip
blocks.html: If you want to catch the sunset from Khao Tang Kuan, aim to start climbing around 17:00 — but check the lift's closing time first. It sometimes closes early. If the lift is shut, the Naga staircase at the back is free to walk up, just a bit more effort.

blocks.text: Food You Shouldn't Skip Along the Way

blocks.html: Songkhla takes its food seriously. The flavours here draw from Chinese, Malay and southern Thai cooking all at once. Below are the dishes that locals think of first — ordered by when you'll likely encounter them on the route above.

items.name: Songkhla Khao Stew
items.blurb: The city's morning ritual — rice ladled into a clear, lightly spiced Chinese-style broth, served with pork or chicken. The old-school spot Kiat Fang on Nang Ngam Road has been doing this for generations. One bowl and you'll understand why locals start every day with it.

items.name: Clay-Pot Ice Cream
items.blurb: Ice cream scooped into small earthenware jars — a Nang Ngam Road tradition that's been cooling down old-town walkers for decades. Simple, cheap, and exactly what you need mid-morning.

items.name: Fish Congee
items.blurb: Silky rice porridge made with fresh fish from Songkhla's waters. Restaurants in the old town get the broth right — mild and comforting, good for breakfast or a late-night bowl.

items.name: Samila Seafood
items.blurb: Mud crab, prawns, fried fish, and sour fish curry from the Gulf of Thailand. Restaurants right on the Samila seafront let you eat with a sea breeze going. Prices depend on the weight of what you order.

items.name: Charcoal-Baked Egg Cakes (Pa Mol)
items.blurb: Traditional southern-style egg cakes baked over charcoal — buttery, crisp outside, soft inside. A Songkhla original that makes a good souvenir to bring home.

items.name: Hat Yai Dim Sum
items.blurb: If you swing through Hat Yai, morning dim sum is non-negotiable. Bao, har gow, siu mai, all dipped in dark soy. Many shops open from 5–6 am and locals pair it with old-school drip coffee.

items.name: Hat Yai Fried Chicken
items.blurb: Crispy-skinned fried chicken topped with fried shallots — Hat Yai's most exported dish. Eat it with sticky rice and you've got a proper meal. Available at markets and dedicated shops around the city.

items.name: Tao Kua Songkhla
items.blurb: A southern-style salad with rice noodles, fried tofu, pork belly, and a sweet-sour dressing. It's the kind of local dish that barely exists outside this area — worth tracking down while you're here.

blocks.title: Honest heads-up
blocks.html: Several popular restaurants in the old town close early and take Mondays off. Some cafes open late. If there's somewhere you're set on visiting, check their hours on Facebook or Google before you leave — it'll save a wasted trip.

blocks.text: Alternative Plan: Hat Yai in One Day (Food & Shopping Focus)

blocks.html: If you only have time in Hat Yai and can't make it out to Songkhla city, you can fill a full day easily. Hat Yai's strengths are food and shopping, with a hilltop city view thrown in. This plan focuses on markets, eating, and a cable car ride.

blocks.label: Hat Yai — 1 Day
blocks.title: Morning dim sum → Park & cable car → Markets → Night market

items.activity: Morning dim sum with old-school drip coffee in Hat Yai
items.note: Dim sum shops in Hat Yai open extremely early — many start from 5–6 am. It's the local way to start the day.

items.activity: Hat Yai Municipal Park — pay respects at the Guan Yin and Phra Phuttha Mongkon Maharaj shrines, then ride the aerial cable car for city views
items.note: The park opens around 06:00–20:00. The cable car is Thailand's first and gives a wide view over the city. Check operating hours at the gate as they vary by day.

items.activity: Lunch — southern Thai rice-and-curry or whatever looks good in the city centre
items.note: Hat Yai has plenty of bold southern curry shops. Go for whichever one has a crowd — that's usually the freshest.

items.activity: Browse Kim Yong Market for food, snacks, imported goods and souvenirs
items.note: Kim Yong is on Sanae Chanon Road in the city centre. It stocks dried goods, snacks, nuts, cosmetics and all manner of gifts. Bargaining is expected.

items.activity: Rest at a cafe or walk around the area near Hat Yai Railway Station
items.note: Use this slot however your energy dictates. If you're tired, go back to the hotel and rest before the night market.

items.activity: Evening at Hat Yai night market — street food and grazing until you're done
items.note: Hat Yai's night food scene covers Thai, Chinese and Malay dishes at wallet-friendly prices. Perfect for an unhurried final meal.

items: Hat Yai to Songkhla city — about 30 km; 30–40 min by car or minivan. Combining both in one day is possible if you get an early start.
Getting around Songkhla city — renting a car or motorbike is the most flexible option. Ride-hailing apps also cover the city centre, and all the main sights are close together.
Best time to visit — the dry season (roughly February to August) means clearer skies. Late in the year (October to December) is wet — keep indoor spots and markets as backup plans.

blocks.text: What to Pack for a Comfortable Day Trip

items: Comfortable walking shoes — the old-town plan involves a lot of walking and some stretches of uneven old pavement.
Umbrella or hat + sunscreen — southern sun is harsh, especially during the afternoon at Samila Beach.
Cash in small bills — many local shops and markets work primarily on cash.
Buffer time for cafes — the old town has a good number of cafes inside beautifully preserved buildings. Leave room in the schedule to sit at one without rushing.

faq.q: Is one day enough for Songkhla?
faq.a: Yes, for the main highlights in the city itself — the three old-town streets, Samila Beach, and Khao Tang Kuan. All of them are within a few kilometres of each other. If you want to explore further out, like Koh Yo island, the lagoon, or nearby waterfalls, two days would be more comfortable.

faq.q: Can I visit Songkhla city as a day trip from Hat Yai?
faq.a: Definitely. It's about 30 km away — roughly 30–40 min by car or minivan. Leave Hat Yai by around 8 am and you'll have time for the old town, Samila, and Khao Tang Kuan before evening, then drive back for dinner in Hat Yai.

faq.q: Does Khao Tang Kuan charge an entry fee? What are the hours?
faq.a: The incline lift costs around THB 30 for adults and THB 20 for children, and runs approximately 08:30–18:00. The Naga staircase at the back is free to walk up any time. Hours can shift, so check before you go — especially if you're planning to stay for sunset.

faq.q: What local food should I try in Songkhla?
faq.a: Songkhla khao stew is the must-have breakfast. Then work through clay-pot ice cream on Nang Ngam Road, fish congee, Samila seafood, and tao kua — a southern-style noodle salad that barely exists outside the area. If you stop in Hat Yai, add morning dim sum and Hat Yai fried chicken.

faq.q: What's the best time of year to visit Songkhla?
faq.a: The dry season, roughly February to August, generally has clearer skies — good for the beach and walking around. Late in the year, October through December, sees heavier rain. If you come during that period, keep some indoor venues and markets in your back pocket as alternatives.
